hints: Start with what you are really finding: magnification = image size divided by actual size, so look carefully at the units of q in cm and r in mm versus the actual size in micrometres.
Remember $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \, \mu\text{m}$, so to turn r into micrometres you multiply by s, then to divide by the actual size of $5 \, \mu\text{m}$ you multiply by $t = \frac{1}{5}$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the golden rule**

Magnification is always image size divided by actual size, but only when both are in the same units.

Key rule:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$

**Convert the image to micrometres**

The actual size is $5 \, \mu\text{m}$. If you measure the image as r in millimetres, you must convert mm to $\mu\text{m}$.

Since $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \, \mu\text{m}$:
$$\text{image in } \mu\text{m} = r \times 1000 = r \times s$$

**Divide by 5 to finish**

Now divide by the actual size of 5:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{r \times s}{5} = r \times s \times \frac{1}{5} = r \times s \times t$$
That matches option D perfectly.

options.A: Uses q in cm but divides by 1000, this converts the wrong way and misses that $1 \text{ cm} = 10000 \, \mu\text{m}$.
options.B: Uses q in cm with x1000, but cm needs x10000 to reach micrometres, so this is 10 times too small.
options.C: Uses r in mm but divides by s, this makes the image smaller instead of converting mm up to micrometres.
options.D: Correctly converts r mm to micrometres with x s (x1000) then divides by 5 using x t (x 1/5).
